vignette:
Mateo describes his life now, at sixty-five, as being too quiet. For forty years, the noise of a bustling school, the structured chaos of bells and chatter, had been a reliable buffer. Now, in the stillness of his small home, the silence is filled with sounds only he can hear. The house creaks, and he’s on his feet. A car backfires down the street, and the sweat on his palms is instantaneous and cold. He has lived in this country for far longer than he lived in his own, but he has never felt safe.

He was nineteen when his life was cleaved in two. He speaks of it in fragments, his gaze fixed on a point on the wall just past my shoulder. It was a jungle, thick and suffocatingly humid, the air heavy with the smell of rot and rain. He and his unit were on patrol, moving through a landscape that was impossibly green and alive. One moment, he was whispering a joke to his friend, Rafael. The next, the world was a percussive roar of gunfire and shouting. He remembers the metallic taste of fear in his mouth, the feeling of the wet earth beneath his cheek, the frantic search for cover that wasn't there. He doesn't remember firing his weapon, but he knows he did. What he remembers with piercing clarity is the sight of Rafael, lying unnaturally still, his eyes open to the canopy above. The ambush was over in minutes, but for Mateo, it has never ended.

He came to the United States a few years later, determined to build a life from the rubble of his youth. He worked, he studied, he learned a new language, and he pushed the jungle into a locked room in his mind. He chose to become a special education teacher, a decision that makes sense to him only in retrospect. He found a deep, anchoring purpose in creating a space of absolute safety for children who were vulnerable. His classroom was a sanctuary of predictability and calm. He was known for his boundless patience, especially with non-verbal students. He could sit for an hour with a child in distress, his presence a steady, quiet reassurance. He was a guardian of quiet rooms and predictable schedules, a fierce protector against the chaos he knew the world was capable of.

This rigid control, however, did not extend to his home. His ex-wife, he says, used to call him a “coiled spring.” He was easily startled, prone to flashes of anger that erupted over trivial things—a dish left in the sink, a change of plans without notice. He could never sit with his back to a door in a restaurant. He avoided crowds and fireworks on the Fourth of July became an annual source of conflict, an ordeal he would endure with a clenched jaw. She said it was like living with a ghost who was always waiting for a fight. The divorce, when it came, felt less like a failure and more like an inevitability. His children are grown and have families of their own, but their calls feel strained. They love him, he knows, but from a careful distance.

Retirement was supposed to be a reward, a time for peace. Instead, it has dismantled the fortress he so carefully constructed. Without the structure of the school day, the memories have breached the walls. A few weeks ago, a sudden, loud fire drill at the school where he was substituting sent him reeling. The shrill, pulsing alarm and flashing lights threw him back forty-five years. He found himself pressed against the classroom wall, heart hammering, the smell of damp earth and cordite filling his senses. He saw the frightened faces of the children and felt a wave of shame so profound it almost brought him to his knees. Now, in his quiet house, he stays up late, watching the street through the blinds, waiting for a threat that has no name, listening to the echoes of an ambush in the settling of an old house.
